About 600 U.S. citizen and 2,800 non-U.S. citizen employees would lose their jobs in the first three years, and U.S. citizen employment would fall 20% in the first five years. About 1,500 Panamanian employees living in the Zone, many of West Indian descent, face particular social difficulties because they are resented by the broader Panamanian public. Panama's two main population centers — Panama City (518,000) and Colon (73,000) — sit at each end of the canal. The reforestation loan targets the rural poor of Panama's Pacific watershed, including thousands of Guaymi Indians in the western central cordillera and poor farmers in the Azuero Peninsula, living on roughly 12,000 square kilometers (about 16% of Panama) of degraded land, with about 5,000 direct beneficiaries.

summary.alternatives_overview.extracted_value: For the treaty, the statement examines four alternatives: taking no action (rejected because Panamanian nationalist pressure would likely produce unrest and worse environmental enforcement), postponing further action (rejected as producing similar instability), implementing the proposed treaty with its environmental provisions (the alternative being pursued), and negotiating a new treaty with stronger environmental safeguards such as giving the Joint Environmental Commission (a joint U.S.–Panama body to review environmental impacts) more power — judged unnecessary and unlikely to be accepted by Panama. Shippers' responses to higher tolls — larger ships, other transport modes, rerouting via the Suez Canal, the Cape of Good Hope, Cape Horn, or the U.S. 'minibridge' (ocean to the West Coast plus rail across the U.S.) — are also analyzed.

summary.environmental_impact.extracted_value: The direct environmental effects of the treaty itself are described as limited — mainly job losses (about 600 U.S. and 2,800 non-U.S. Canal Company employees in the first three years) and up to a 10% annual diversion of canal traffic to other routes. The larger concern is indirect: most of the Canal Zone is 'an island of forest in the midst of a generally cleared countryside,' and if Panama cannot enforce protections, slash-and-burn squatting could silt the canal, threaten Panama City's drinking water from Madden Lake, and harm endangered species — 8 U.S.-listed species occur on Barro Colorado Island (a 6,000-acre Smithsonian biological reserve) and in the Pipeline Road area, and these areas hold 5% of the world's and 20% of the Americas' endangered mammals. Other sensitive areas include the 3,500-acre Madden Forest Preserve, Farfan Marsh, and the Fort Sherman–Achiote Road area. A rise in insect-borne disease, especially malaria, is flagged if sanitation is under-funded. Canal-widening dredging in the Chagres basin/Lake Gatún area would damage or bury pre-Columbian and Colonial archaeological sites (Frijoles will be completely covered by dump spoil), though the consultant judges most sites already so disturbed that the incremental loss is modest. The 50% cumulative tolls increase, by contrast, is projected to have no significant environmental impact: ship transits would drop less than 6.2% by 1985, only about 4,456,000 tons of cargo would move on longer routes (adding roughly 20,776 tons of fuel), and diversion to U.S. rail 'minibridge' would add about 1,099 short tons of pollutants against 205.2 million tons of total U.S. emissions in 1973. Attachments compile applicable pollution-control laws, including the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (which bars oil discharges in navigable waters), Canal Zone rules against dumping ballast or garbage in canal waters, and Panama's Decree No. 23 of 1967, which flatly bans hunting of listed species including white-tailed deer, tapir, quetzal, harpy eagle, manatee, and green sea turtle. The Panama reforestation loan responds to already-severe damage — erosion that in some areas 'has become irreversible' and threatens future urban water supplies, hydroelectric generation, irrigation, and 'even threatens the watershed area which feeds the canal.'

summary.overview.extracted_value: This 1977 State Department environmental impact statement covers a package of related actions: a proposed new Panama Canal Treaty (with a companion neutrality treaty) under which the United States would gradually turn the Canal Zone — a strip of Panamanian territory five miles wide on either side of the canal — over to Panama by December 31, 1999, while continuing to operate and defend the 51-mile lock canal; a proposed roughly 19.5% across-the-board increase in canal tolls; and a proposed AID loan to help Panama protect the forested watershed the canal depends on. The people most directly affected are the roughly 13,000–14,000 Canal Company/Canal Zone Government employees (about 27% U.S. citizens and the rest almost all Panamanian) and their families, U.S. military personnel at seven bases in the Zone, users of the canal on major trade routes, U.S. Atlantic and Gulf port workers, and the rural poor of Panama's Pacific watershed including thousands of Guaymi Indians. Alternatives considered include taking no action, postponing the treaty, negotiating a treaty with stronger environmental provisions, and — for the tolls action — either cutting canal operating costs or asking Congress to shift the operating cost from canal users to the U.S. Treasury. Direct environmental effects of the treaty itself are described as limited, but the drafters flag two large indirect risks: deforestation of lands handed to Panama, which would silt the canal and threaten Panama City's drinking water from Madden Lake, and a possible rise in insect-borne disease, especially malaria, if sanitation is not adequately funded; the tolls increase, meanwhile, is projected to divert only a small share of cargo and to have no significant environmental impact. Public reaction reflected in the document includes deep Panamanian resentment of the 1903 arrangement (negotiations followed 1964 rioting in which 20 Panamanians and 4 Americans were killed), strong opposition to toll-driven cargo diversion from East and Gulf Coast port interests and the longshoremen's union, and comments solicited from federal agencies, the Government of Panama, and conservation groups including the Audubon Society, Sierra Club, and World Wildlife Fund.

The figure '13,000–14,000' is an approximation of the document's stated 13,139, which falls within the range; the 'roughly' qualifier makes this acceptable. summary.project_description.extracted_value: The U.S. Department of State is proposing to conclude a new Panama Canal Treaty with the Republic of Panama, along with a companion treaty guaranteeing the canal's permanent neutrality, to replace the 1903 treaty under which the United States has administered the Canal Zone (a strip of Panamanian territory five miles wide on either side of the canal). Under the basic treaty, the U.S. would continue to operate and defend the 51-mile lock canal until December 31, 1999, while gradually transferring commercial activities, housing, and lands outside the operating area to Panama. Two related actions are also covered: a proposed roughly 19.5% across-the-board increase in canal tolls (from $1.08 to $1.29 per Panama Canal net ton laden, and from $0.86 to $1.03 in ballast) required by the statutory tolls formula, and a proposed AID loan (about $20 million total, half from Panama) to reforest roughly 75,000 hectares in Panama's central watersheds and protect the water supply the canal depends on.

summary.public_response.extracted_value: The State Department shortened the standard 45-day comment period to 30 days, with the concurrence of the Council on Environmental Quality chairman, to keep the impact statement relevant to Senate consideration; comments were solicited from federal agencies, the Government of Panama, and conservation groups including the Audubon Society, Sierra Club, Nature Conservancy, and World Wildlife Fund. The document records that the 1903 arrangement is 'deeply resented in Panama' and that negotiations began after 1964 rioting along the Canal Zone boundary in which 20 Panamanians and 4 Americans were killed, with talks spanning four U.S. administrations of both parties over thirteen years. Existing concerns cited include worries in 'some quarters' that annuity payments to Panama might leave inadequate funding for environmental enforcement, Panamanian press criticism of Canal Zone arrests of illegal hunters, and earlier criticism by environmental and scientific groups of the 1970 Interoceanic Canal Commission's conclusions on a sea-level canal. On the tolls action, the strongest opposition came from East and Gulf Coast port interests — the Council of North Atlantic Shipping Associations, the International Longshoremen's Association, the Delaware River Port Authority, and the Massachusetts Port Authority — who argued that higher tolls would divert cargo to rail 'minibridge,' raising energy use and air pollution and cutting longshore jobs; the assessment notes these claims were 'not supported by any quantitative analysis' and that a U.S. District Court had found 'no adequate demonstration of any physical harm or injury.' Sea-Land disagreed with those port and union groups on environmental effects.

extracted_value.claim: This is an environmental impact statement for a foreign-policy treaty — the transfer of the Panama Canal and its surrounding Canal Zone to Panama — rather than for a physical construction project, and the State Department cut the normal public comment period from 45 days to 30 days to keep the document 'relevant to Senate consideration' of the treaty.
extracted_value.evidence_quote: The period for comment on this draft has been reduced from the usual 45 days to 30 days. We are seeking to prepare the impact statement in time to be relevant to Senate consideration of the proposed treaty.
extracted_value.why_notable: Applying National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) to a bilateral treaty is itself atypical, and compressing the public comment window to fit the Senate's ratification calendar subordinates the environmental review process to a diplomatic schedule.
